The number on your stub is not the number they owe you

California pays overtime on your regular rate, not your hourly rate. A bonus changes it. Almost no pay stub shows it. Backpay computes what the Labor Code required, week by week, and names the section behind every figure.

0.5%

of stolen wages get recovered

Between $40 and $60 billion a year is taken from American workers in unpaid wages. Over thirteen years the Department of Labor recovered $3.28 billion of it. Against the midpoint estimate for that period, that is one half of one percent.

Computed from the DOL Wage and Hour Division enforcement file, FY2013 to FY2025, held at research/data/dol-whd-allacts-fy2013-2025.csv.

Two people need this arithmetic, and only one of them can pay for it

A worker needs to know whether one paycheck was short. A law firm needs the same computation run across two hundred workers and four years, in a form an opposing expert can attack and a judge can follow.

It is the same engine. The worker's version is free and always will be, because charging someone to find out whether they were robbed inverts the point of the exercise. The firm's version is the business.

For the worker

Enter the hours and what you were paid. Get back what the law required, week by week, with the section number behind each line. No account, no employer contact, nothing kept unless you ask.

For the firm

Import payroll records, model a class, export a schedule where every dollar traces to a statute. Priced against the paralegal hours it replaces, not against other software.

For legal aid and worker centres

The same tool the firms use, free, because you already sit in front of exactly these workers and are chronically under-resourced.

One ordinary week, taken apart

Nothing about this schedule looks like theft. Five normal days, one long one, a short Sunday, a production bonus. It is the shape of a warehouse week, and it is short by $207.64.

Repeat that week across a 96-week class period and one worker is owed $19,933.44. A class of two hundred is owed just under four million. That is the arithmetic a paralegal currently does by hand, in a spreadsheet, for every named plaintiff, and it is what gets checked line by line in a motion for class certification.

−49%

in federal compliance actions since 2013

Compliance actions fell from 33,146 to 16,924. Workers receiving back wages fell by a third. The money recovered stayed flat. Read those three together and the picture is an agency running fewer, larger cases, which means the small individual claim is what got squeezed out. That claim is this product's entire subject.

Same file. Thirteen fiscal years, counted directly.

The questions people actually ask first

Is this free for workers, or free until it isn't?
Free. Not a trial, not a freemium tier with the answer behind a card. The workers this serves are the least able to pay of anyone involved, and the business is funded by the law firms who need the same arithmetic at scale.
Will my employer find out I used this?
No. Backpay never contacts an employer, and it has no way to. It reads hours and pay that you enter and computes what the Labor Code required. What you do with that is entirely yours.
Is Backpay a law firm?
No, and it will not act like one. It does arithmetic and cites the section behind each figure. Whether you have a claim worth bringing is a question for a lawyer, and the answer depends on facts arithmetic cannot see.
What happens when the law does not fit?
It refuses to answer and says why. An alternative workweek schedule, a collective bargaining agreement, piece-rate pay or an exempt classification each change the calculation in ways this engine does not model. A tool that overstates a claim is worse than no tool, because an overstated claim is what gets a whole damages model thrown out.

Backpay is software. It is not a law firm, it does not give legal advice, and it does not represent anyone.
